samples.text: Valuation is running on a manual footing for now. The current basis is manual agency code mapping override applied to complete valuation for the period. That override is a stopgap. Engineers apply it one code at a time, against legacy and cloud code sets that are not interchangeable. It keeps the period moving, but it depends on engineers applying the right code by hand, and every override is a fresh chance to repeat the original error. The reason a stopgap is needed has been confirmed: stale legacy-to-new agency code mapping in the reference data register. Until that register entry is corrected and checked, the override stays in place. Readers deciding whether to wait should weigh the two facts against each other. The cause is known and contained to one table, which argues for patience. The fix in place, though, is manual and unreviewed, so output produced under it carries more risk than normal and should be spot-checked before anyone builds on it. The valuation failure has one established cause: stale legacy-to-new agency code mapping in the reference data register. Nothing in the platform itself broke. That finding replaced an earlier working view. When the incident opened, the cause was recorded as overnight ERP outage, and the response team spent its first hours treating an upstream interruption as the likely explanation. That view did not survive the evidence. A direct read of the upstream records ruled it out: ERP logs show no interruption during the valuation window. With the upstream system cleared, the team turned to the reference data that feeds the inventory valuation service, and the stale entry was found there. Behind the stale entry sits a weaker control, now classified as control failure: the mapping table has no registered owner and no required reviewer. The distinction matters for the record, because the first theory sent effort to the wrong team and cost the morning.
